item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Thursday, May 14th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

We start with the foreign policy story that keeps spilling directly into gas prices, inflation expectations, mortgage pressure, and the market's daily mood. The Trump-Xi summit is now underway in Beijing, and the continuity from yesterday still holds: this is not a resolution story yet. It is still a proof story.

The Associated Press reports that Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping opened their meetings with sharp differences still plainly visible, especially over Taiwan, trade, and the war with Iran. Xi warned that mishandling Taiwan could lead to conflict, while investors kept watching for any sign that the two leaders could lower tensions elsewhere. That is the key point this morning. The summit matters not because it guarantees a breakthrough, but because the market badly wants evidence that the two biggest powers can at least keep multiple crises from getting worse at the same time.

AP's broader markets coverage says world shares mostly rose as investors watched the summit, but the tone was cautious rather than celebratory. That fits the larger continuity line. The market is still looking for something more concrete than ceremony. On the Iran side, the question remains whether diplomacy can produce anything that visibly improves commercial confidence around energy flows and shipping risk. On the China side, the question is whether the summit reduces friction or simply contains it for another news cycle.

For listeners, the practical reading is unchanged. If the Strait of Hormuz still looks vulnerable, energy stays expensive. If energy stays expensive, inflation stays harder to cool. And if inflation stays harder to cool, the path to meaningfully lower borrowing costs stays narrow. So watch the actual evidence today: not the handshakes, but whether shipping, insurance, and oil-market behavior show any real improvement.

National story number two reaches its decision point today. The Supreme Court's temporary order preserving broad access to mifepristone runs through Thursday, May 14th. The Associated Press reported on Monday, May 11th, that Justice Samuel Alito's order kept pharmacy, mail, and telehealth access in place while the justices considered whether new restrictions should take effect. Yesterday, that was a countdown story. Today, it is a deadline story.

That matters because the Court is no longer just buying time. It now has to decide whether to preserve the status quo longer or allow a major operational shift in abortion access. The legal stakes remain broader than this one drug. If courts become more willing to override the Food and Drug Administration's long-standing regulatory framework, that would ripple beyond abortion into the basic question of how medicines are governed in the United States.

So the continuity language here is simple. Yesterday the cliff was tomorrow. Today the cliff is today. If the Court extends access again, the immediate disruption is delayed. If it does not, providers, patients, pharmacies, and states could be forced into a rapid adjustment almost immediately.

National story number three is the Senate Republican immigration enforcement package, which still deserves attention because it is moving from slogan politics into real budget politics. Roll Call's detailed reporting remains the clearest guide here: the package comes to about 69.2 billion dollars, with the biggest shares aimed at Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection. Roll Call also reports the committees tentatively plan markups for Monday, May 19th, which puts this squarely inside the next five-day window.

The Associated Press adds another layer of friction. Republican senators are still asking for more detail on a separate 1 billion dollar White House security request tied to the broader package, including funds connected to President Trump's East Wing ballroom security needs. That matters because once a bill gets specific, internal cost questions get louder. This is where a party that agrees on tougher enforcement still has to answer how much it wants to spend, how quickly, and on what exact mix of detention, hiring, border operations, and security add-ons.

So the watch item here is whether leaders can keep the package focused enough to move, or whether side fights over cost and White House extras make the politics messier before markups begin next week.

Back in Columbus, the most important local continuity story is still Issue 5, and this morning the lack of a dramatic new announcement is itself part of the story. Axios Columbus has already established the scale of the mandate: voters approved the emergency-response charter amendment by a huge margin. That means the politics of persuasion are over. The politics of execution have started.

The core question has not changed since yesterday. When does City Hall move from supportive language to operational language. Who owns the rollout. What milestones get published first. How will dispatch rules be written. What staffing and clinical partnerships are needed. And how transparent will the city be now that the campaign is over and the public expects proof, not applause. In these transitional civic stories, silence has a shelf life. The public usually gives leaders a short grace period after a win, but not a long one.

The other local pressure point remains housing stress and homelessness. Axios Columbus reported last week that Franklin County's point-in-time count found a record 2,587 people experiencing homelessness. That number is still shaping the local conversation because nothing in the underlying affordability math has changed enough to ease it. High borrowing costs, elevated home prices, and limited room for lower-cost development inside the county are still pushing pressure outward and downward at the same time.

One fresh Ohio legal story also belongs on your radar this morning because it started in Franklin County and will keep moving. WOSU reported late Tuesday that the lawsuit over Ohio's EdChoice private-school voucher program is headed to the appeals court after a Franklin County Common Pleas judge found the program unconstitutional but allowed it to continue while litigation proceeds. For Central Ohio listeners, that is a reminder that some of the state's most consequential policy fights are still being shaped in local courts before they become statewide election issues.

On home lending and mortgages, the message this morning is that demand is holding up better than relief is. The Mortgage Bankers Association said Wednesday that mortgage applications rose 1.7 percent in the latest weekly survey, with purchase applications up 4 percent from the prior week and 7 percent above the same week a year earlier. But MBA also said the average contract rate on a conforming 30-year loan rose to 6.46 percent, the highest in five weeks.

That is the housing-market split-screen right now. Buyers are still showing up, but they are showing up in a rate environment that keeps the monthly-payment test severe. Freddie Mac's most recent official weekly benchmark, released May 7th, put the 30-year fixed at 6.37 percent. So whether you use the Freddie Mac benchmark or the more immediate MBA application data, the same conclusion holds: mortgage costs are still high enough to dominate the spring market.

That remains a Columbus story, not just a national one. When rates stay in the mid-sixes, affordability keeps nudging buyers toward surrounding counties, smaller homes, or delayed decisions. So the continuity line from yesterday remains intact. This is still less a confidence problem than a monthly-payment problem.

In AI and technology, the most important shift is that Washington still agrees advanced AI needs more scrutiny, but it still does not agree on the machinery. Axios reported yesterday that White House AI executive action is stalled by internal infighting and time pressure, even as lawmakers are pressing for faster action on cyber risks tied to frontier models. One of the live fights is over where advanced model testing should sit: in a more civilian standards process or deeper inside the national security apparatus.

That matters because the private sector is not waiting for the government to get tidy. AI remains an infrastructure story as much as a software story. The Associated Press reported that technology stocks, led again by Nvidia and other AI-linked names, helped push the S and P 500 and Nasdaq to fresh records on Wednesday even after discouraging inflation data. In other words, investors are still rewarding AI exposure, but Washington is still struggling to define the guardrails.

That is where the national and local storylines meet. Central Ohio remains deeply tied to the physical side of this buildout: data centers, power, water, logistics, semiconductors, and the longer confidence cycle around Intel's Ohio project. Axios Columbus reported this week that Intel's Ohio story has regained some momentum as the company reaffirms production timing and leans into the broader AI boom. So the AI watch item today is not just who launches the next model. It is who gets trusted, who gets tested, and which regions can physically support the next wave of demand.

The markets snapshot this morning reflects that same tension between momentum and caution. The Associated Press says the S and P 500 rose 0.6 percent on Wednesday to a record 7,444.25, the Nasdaq climbed 1.2 percent to a record 26,402.34, and the Dow slipped 0.1 percent to 49,693.20. The driver was a rebound in technology stocks, especially AI-linked names, even though inflation at the wholesale level came in hotter than economists expected.

That is an important signal. The rally is still broad enough to keep confidence alive, but it is not carefree. Markets are effectively saying they still believe in earnings and AI, but they are also acknowledging that inflation pressure has not disappeared. So the market's posture this morning is not simple risk-on euphoria. It is confidence with a stress fracture running through it.

If oil stays elevated, if yields remain firm, or if geopolitics worsens, that fracture gets wider fast. If those pressures ease, the market can keep treating inflation as annoying rather than decisive. That is why the summit in Beijing, the oil story, and the mortgage story all still connect.

For Columbus weather, today looks much more usable than yesterday. The National Weather Service forecast for Columbus calls for clouds early, then gradual clearing, with a high near 64 and a northwest breeze. Tonight turns mostly clear with a low around 44. Friday warms back up with a high near 72, and the weekend trends much warmer, with thunderstorm chances returning late Friday night into Saturday before temperatures push toward the upper 80s and even the 90s early next week.

So the practical advice is simple: today is your lighter-jacket day, Friday is the payoff, and the weekend starts the turn toward much warmer air.

The through-line this morning is that nearly every major story is testing whether institutions can turn posture into proof. The Trump-Xi summit matters if it lowers real-world risk, not if it just produces photos. The Supreme Court's mifepristone pause matters because today forces a decision or another extension. Senate Republicans have a real immigration bill on paper, which means the cost and process fights get more serious from here. Columbus voters gave Issue 5 a mandate, and now city leadership has to show the machinery. Franklin County's housing and homelessness pressures are still demanding an answer bigger than rhetoric. Mortgage demand is hanging in, but rates are still high enough to do real damage to affordability. Washington wants an AI posture, but still has not settled on an AI process. And markets are climbing, but under pressure from the same inflation and geopolitical forces we opened with.

So watch these points today: any sign that the Beijing summit reduces actual geopolitical or oil-market stress, any Supreme Court move on mifepristone before the Thursday deadline ends, any clearer signal on how Senate Republicans will handle the immigration package and its cost questions, any visible implementation detail from Columbus on Issue 5, any stronger regional response to housing and homelessness pressure, whether mortgage rates keep buyers active or push them outward again, whether Washington's AI infighting starts to resolve, and whether markets can hold record territory with inflation and oil still hanging over them.

That is your Morning Brief for Thursday, May 14th. Have a good morning, enjoy the cooler air while it lasts, and keep an eye on the stories that are running out of room to stay unresolved.

Good morning. It is Wednesday, May 13th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

We start again with the story that still touches foreign policy, inflation, gas prices, mortgage rates, and the broader market all at once. The Iran ceasefire story is still not a resolution story. It is still a proof story. Overnight, Reuters reported that oil slipped after a three-day rally, but only because traders were waiting to see whether anything real comes from the next phase of diplomacy as President Trump heads into a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The underlying condition has not improved enough to calm markets. Brent was still near 107 dollars a barrel and U.S. crude was still just above 101 in early trading, which tells you the market still sees serious supply risk.

That is the continuity point from yesterday. We said the real test was not the language of diplomacy but the condition of the Strait of Hormuz. That remains true this morning. The Associated Press reports Trump is leaving for Beijing with the war and its economic fallout hanging over the trip, even as he publicly says he does not need China to help end the conflict. That matters because the White House is still trying to project leverage while markets are still pricing in disruption.

The practical read for listeners is straightforward. If shipping risk through Hormuz remains elevated, oil stays expensive. If oil stays expensive, inflation pressure lingers. And if inflation pressure lingers, the hoped-for path toward lower borrowing costs gets harder again. So the watch item today is not whether officials talk about peace. It is whether there is any visible change in commercial traffic, insurance costs, or broader market confidence around the waterway that moves about a fifth of the world's oil.

National story number two is the abortion pill case at the Supreme Court, where the key update is still the calendar. On Monday, May 11th, Justice Samuel Alito extended nationwide access to mifepristone through at least Thursday, May 14th, according to the Associated Press. That means the current system, including mail and pharmacy access, is still in place for now. But the extension did not answer the underlying question. It just moved the moment of decision.

That makes today less about a legal surprise and more about a countdown. Providers, patients, and state officials have a little time, but not much certainty. The case still matters on two levels. First, it is an abortion access fight with immediate consequences for how people obtain care. Second, it is a test of how much courts may allow states to interfere with federal drug regulation. If the Food and Drug Administration's authority becomes easier to override in court, that is not just an abortion story. That becomes a broader institutional story about how medicines are governed in the United States.

So the continuity language here is simple. Yesterday the Court delayed the cliff. Today the cliff is still there, just closer. Between now and Thursday, the only question that really matters is whether the justices preserve the status quo longer or allow a disruptive new set of restrictions to take effect.

National story number three is the Senate immigration enforcement push. Roll Call's reporting remains the cleanest frame here. Senate Republicans have now released text for a package worth about 69.2 billion dollars, with roughly 39.2 billion from Judiciary and more than 26 billion for Customs and Border Protection, plus major new funding for ICE and related operations. The reason this still belongs in the brief is that the fight is no longer rhetorical. It is now a specific argument over money, staffing, detention capacity, technology, and the scale of a long-duration enforcement buildout.

That specificity changes the politics. Once the bill is real, cost questions become harder to dodge, and procedural fights become sharper. The Associated Press also reported fresh Republican discomfort around attaching White House security requests to the broader package, which is a reminder that even when a party agrees on the headline goal, the details can still create friction. So watch two things here. Watch whether Democrats are able to slow or narrow the package procedurally, and watch whether any Republican concerns about cost or unrelated add-ons become more public before the next floor moves.

Back in Columbus, the main civic continuity story is still Issue 5. Voters approved the emergency-response charter amendment last week with 77 percent support, according to Axios Columbus, and that means the campaign phase is over. The implementation phase is the story now. That is where credibility will be built or lost.

Nothing overnight changed that basic frame, which is important in itself. There has not yet been a dramatic new rollout announcement, and in a story like this, silence becomes part of the story pretty quickly. The public has already said yes. So the next test is whether city leaders move from broad support language into operational language. Who is responsible for designing the system. How will dispatch criteria be written. What does staffing look like. When do interim milestones get published. And how visible will the city keep this effort now that the election is over.

Large victories create large expectations. A 77 percent result does not buy much patience for vague follow-through. So for the next few days, listen closely for any concrete timeline, named leadership structure, or budget clarity. That will tell you whether this becomes one of Columbus's durable reform stories or another broadly popular idea that drifts once the votes are counted.

The other local pressure point that still deserves continuity treatment is housing stress. Axios Columbus reported that Franklin County's point-in-time homelessness count reached a record 2,587 people this year, the fourth straight annual high. That was not an overnight development, but it remains one of the most important local facts on the board because it is likely to keep shaping politics in the days ahead. This is one of those stories where the update is not a new number every morning. The update is whether leaders start behaving as if the number changed the urgency.

That is why it stays active. Columbus keeps talking about growth, investment, and development, but this record count is a reminder that growth is not being experienced evenly. If there is a meaningful local response soon, it will likely show up in shelter strategy, supportive housing commitments, or stronger public messaging from city and county officials. If not, the homelessness figure remains an indictment hanging over every prosperity headline.

There is also a fresh Central Ohio business note that fits both the local economy and the national tech story. Axios Columbus reported Tuesday that Intel's Ohio project is regaining momentum, at least politically and psychologically, after a long stretch of doubt. Intel has already spent about 5 billion dollars on the Ohio One project, reaffirmed a plan to begin production by 2031, and is benefiting from a rebound in sentiment as its stock recovers. That does not erase the delays. But it does change the mood.

Why does that matter to this brief. Because it reinforces the idea that the Central Ohio growth story is still deeply tied to chips, infrastructure, and long-horizon technology bets. It also tells you local leaders still see advanced manufacturing and compute capacity as foundational to the region's future, even when timelines slip. So keep Intel in the Columbus watch list not as a ribbon-cutting story, but as a confidence story. If the momentum holds, it strengthens the broader argument that Central Ohio remains central to the next phase of American tech infrastructure.

On home lending and mortgage affordability, the latest weekly benchmark still comes from Freddie Mac's May 7th survey, which put the average 30-year fixed at 6.37 percent, up from 6.30 percent the week before. Since then, daily market-based readings tracked by major outlets have kept the 30-year rate in roughly the mid-6 percent range. The bigger picture has not changed. Rates are not back at the peak pain of prior years, but they remain high enough to keep affordability firmly in control of the housing conversation.

That matters nationally and locally. Axios Columbus has already shown that Central Ohio home sales have been shifting toward surrounding counties as Franklin County prices stay elevated. Higher borrowing costs reinforce that shift because they make monthly payment math even less forgiving inside the urban core. And the oil story loops back in here too. When energy prices rise and Treasury yields stay firm, mortgage relief gets harder to find.

So the mortgage continuity line for today is this. Inventory is somewhat better than in the tightest years, but affordability is still doing most of the decision-making. For many buyers, this is still not a confidence problem. It is a monthly-payment problem. Until rates move down more decisively, the spring market remains active but constrained.

In AI and technology, the story keeps getting more strategic and more physical at the same time. Axios reported this morning that internal White House disagreements are slowing federal AI executive action even as pressure grows for clearer national rules. That fits neatly with Reuters reporting from last week that Microsoft, Google, and xAI agreed to give the U.S. government early access to frontier models for security reviews. Put together, those two developments tell you Washington increasingly agrees that advanced AI needs scrutiny, but it still has not settled on the machinery for how that scrutiny should work.

That uncertainty matters because the market is moving ahead anyway. Reuters also reported recently that OpenAI- and Anthropic-linked ventures are trying to acquire services firms that help companies actually deploy AI inside real organizations. That is an important shift. The competition is no longer just about who has the smartest model. It is also about who can pass security review, who can integrate inside big institutions, and who can supply the compute, power, water, and engineering labor needed to operate at scale.

That is why this remains a Columbus story too, not just a Silicon Valley story. Central Ohio's infrastructure questions around data centers, water use, power demand, Intel, and logistics all sit inside that broader AI buildout. So the AI watch item today is not just product launches. It is governance plus infrastructure. Who gets trusted. Who gets reviewed. Who can deploy. And who can physically support the next wave of demand.

The markets snapshot this morning is a little less euphoric than it was at the start of the week. The Associated Press says that on Tuesday, May 12th, the S and P 500 slipped 0.2 percent to 7,400.96, the Nasdaq fell 0.7 percent to 26,088.20, and the Dow added 0.1 percent to 49,760.56. That follows Monday's record closes for the S and P and Nasdaq. So the broad picture is still one of strength, but the mood is no longer simply straight up.

The reason matters. The AP and Reuters both tied the pressure to a combination of higher oil prices, firmer inflation concern, and a pullback in some of the AI-linked stocks that had driven so much recent momentum. Treasury yields stayed elevated too, with the 10-year around the mid-4.4 percent range. That tells you investors are still willing to own growth, but they are becoming more sensitive to the idea that inflation could stay sticky for longer than they want.

So the best reading for markets this morning is selective confidence. The rally is not broken, but it is being tested by the same forces we opened with: energy, geopolitics, and the cost of money. If those pressures intensify, the market narrative changes quickly from record highs to resilience under strain.

For Columbus weather, the practical message is that the wettest part of this stretch is moving through, but the day stays unsettled and cooler. The latest forecast calls for a chance of showers Wednesday, especially early, with a high in the upper 50s to upper 60s depending on where you are in the metro, plus brisk west to north winds. Tonight turns cooler with lows near 40, and Thursday looks drier and brighter with sun returning and highs in the mid-50s.

So plan for a breezy cooldown today. If you were hoping for a clean spring day, Thursday looks like the better payoff.

The through-line this morning is that the biggest stories are still asking for evidence. The Iran ceasefire only matters if shipping risk actually improves. The Supreme Court's mifepristone order only matters until the justices decide what comes next, and that deadline is now basically tomorrow. Senate Republicans have real immigration numbers on paper, which means the fiscal and procedural fight gets more serious. Columbus voters delivered a mandate on Issue 5, so now implementation has to become visible. Record homelessness keeps testing whether local growth is broad enough to matter. Mortgage rates remain high enough to dominate affordability. Intel's recovery story is helping restore confidence in Ohio's tech future, but it still has to prove itself over a much longer runway. And AI keeps moving from novelty toward governance and infrastructure.

So watch these points today: any real sign that the Strait of Hormuz is becoming safer for commercial traffic, any signal from the Supreme Court before the Thursday, May 14th mifepristone deadline, any new procedural movement on the Senate immigration package, any concrete implementation detail from Columbus on Issue 5, any stronger public response to the Franklin County homelessness count, whether mortgage pressure keeps pushing buyers outward, whether Intel's renewed momentum holds, and whether markets keep tolerating higher oil and higher yields.

That is your Morning Brief for Wednesday, May 13th. Have a good morning, keep a jacket handy for the wind and cooler air, and stay focused on the stories that are moving from promises into proof.

They feel it when gasoline rises, when freight costs stay firm, when inflation expectations creep up, and when interest rate relief keeps getting delayed. For today, the thing to watch is simple: not whether officials say talks continue, but whether there is visible evidence that commercial movement through Hormuz is getting safer and more normal.

So this remains both a rights story and an institutional power story. We flagged this yesterday as a move from message politics into governing detail, and that is still the right frame.

It also becomes a test of whether Republicans can keep internal unity around a very large enforcement expansion while the public is still focused on affordability. Watch for procedural attacks from Democrats, but also watch for whether cost concerns inside the GOP become louder now that the real numbers are on paper.

Axios Columbus reported that Issue 5 passed with 77 percent support and sets up a path toward round-the-clock non-police response options for some nonviolent 911 calls, with rollout goals beginning in 2028 and fuller implementation by 2030.

The political campaign is over. The hard part starts now. This is where implementation stories get won or lost. The questions are no longer whether voters liked the idea. The questions are who owns the rollout, how dispatch criteria are defined, how quickly staffing plans are built, how funding scales over time, and whether City Hall keeps public momentum alive now that the ballot energy is gone.

That shift matters because Issue 5 passed so decisively that a weak follow-through would stand out immediately. Big margins create big expectations. So over the next several days, listen for early signs of administrative seriousness. If city leaders start naming timelines, leadership structure, and near-term milestones, the story will feel durable. If the post-election message gets vague, skepticism will return quickly.

Axios Columbus noted Monday that the reckless homicide conviction is unusual for an officer-involved shooting case, but it also leaves a major unresolved question because the jury did not agree on the murder charge. That means the case produced accountability, but not full closure.

That distinction is important. A conviction changes the conversation, but it does not end it. The next thing to watch is whether prosecutors say anything soon about retrying the unresolved count, or whether the legal system effectively signals that the reckless homicide verdict is where this story will end before July sentencing. Either answer would carry civic weight in Columbus, because this case has always been about more than one courtroom result. It has also been about public trust.

The broader housing pressure story in Franklin County is still active too. Axios Columbus reported last week that the latest point-in-time count reached a record 2,587 people experiencing homelessness in Franklin County, the fourth straight annual high. Even though that report is not brand new this morning, it remains one of the most important local trend lines because it is unlikely to leave the agenda quickly.

Columbus is talking about public safety reform, major development, and infrastructure demands tied to growth, but the affordability crisis is still getting worse at the household level. Record homelessness means the housing debate is no longer abstract. If leaders respond, the signs will likely show up in shelter capacity, supportive housing commitments, or a more urgent public framing from city and county officials. If they do not, this data point will keep hanging over every growth narrative in the region.

And because oil is back above 100 dollars and Treasury yields moved up again Monday, the mortgage story remains connected to the same global pressure we opened with.

This time, Meade did not testify, and both sides closed by trying to give jurors a cleaner version of the case. Prosecutors argue the evidence does not support self-defense. The defense argues Meade faced a threat when Goodson, who was legally armed, allegedly pointed a gun.

As of this morning, the watch item is simply the verdict timeline. Once a jury has the case, the tone can change fast. A verdict would instantly become the dominant local story because of what it says about accountability, public trust, and one of the Columbus area's highest-profile police shooting cases. If deliberations stretch out, that itself becomes a signal that jurors are working through the same core tension that complicated the first trial.

In housing and mortgage news, the number to know this morning is 6.37 percent. Freddie Mac says the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose from 6.30 percent last week to 6.37 percent this week, while the 15-year fixed moved up to 5.72 percent.

The continuity line we have been tracking is still intact. Housing is not collapsing, but affordability remains extremely fragile. Rates are below where they were a year ago, and Freddie Mac says higher inventory and softer new-home prices may modestly help buyers. But the market is still being pushed around by yields, oil, and inflation expectations. That means one geopolitical shock can still ripple all the way into a monthly payment in Central Ohio.

The practical takeaway is that the spring market is still alive, but it is not comfortable. Buyers may have more choices than they did in recent years, yet financing costs remain high enough that even a small move higher can change what households qualify for. So the thing to watch next is whether bond-market relief from falling oil can actually stick, or whether rates stay lodged in the mid-sixes and keep the season constrained.

In AI and technology, there are really two connected stories this morning. The first is the market story. Reuters reports that AMD's strong outlook helped drive another rally in chip stocks as investors keep betting that AI demand is broadening beyond the original leaders. The second is the enterprise distribution story, where OpenAI's expanded presence on Amazon Bedrock continues to underline that the real AI contest is increasingly about where advanced models live inside existing cloud and software ecosystems.

That fits the continuity we have been following. The center of gravity in AI keeps moving away from novelty and toward deployment. Investors are rewarding companies tied to chips, infrastructure, and enterprise access because those are the places where real spending is easiest to defend. If AMD can convince the market that AI demand is spreading into a wider chip set, that helps explain the persistent enthusiasm across the sector. And if advanced models and coding tools are easier to consume inside AWS, that lowers friction for companies that want AI without rebuilding their stack around a single vendor.

So the watch item here is whether the next phase of the AI story is more about platform control than model theater. The companies with the best distribution, best compute access, and best enterprise workflow integration may end up shaping the next leg of adoption even more than the companies with the flashiest demo.

That brings us to the markets snapshot. Wednesday was a strong risk-on session. The Associated Press says the S and P 500 rose 1.5 percent to a record 7,365.12, the Dow climbed to 49,910.59, the Nasdaq jumped 2 percent to 25,838.94, and the Russell 2000 also pushed to a fresh high. The main drivers were hopes for de-escalation with Iran and renewed AI enthusiasm after AMD's results.

This morning the tone is still constructive, but it is fragile in a very specific way. Reuters says the S and P 500 and Nasdaq touched fresh records again in early Thursday trading while oil kept falling on hopes of a U.S.-Iran peace agreement. The Associated Press said Brent crude dropped below 97 dollars a barrel Thursday morning after being above 115 earlier this week.

That is the market setup in one sentence: stocks like the idea of peace and cheaper oil, but they are still trading on a confidence problem rather than a solved problem. If Hormuz really moves toward normal shipping, lower oil can ease inflation pressure, support bonds, and help mortgage markets. If the diplomacy slips or the shipping reality does not improve, this very upbeat market can reprice quickly.

So the thing to watch in markets today is whether investors keep rewarding the same combination of falling energy prices and AI optimism, or whether they start demanding harder evidence that the geopolitical story is actually stabilizing. In this environment, oil is not just an energy chart. It is almost the master risk signal.

For Columbus weather, today looks quieter and cooler than the stormy pattern from earlier in the week. National Weather Service forecasts around the Columbus area point to a dry Thursday with highs generally in the upper 50s to low 60s, then a milder Friday before showers return late Friday night and into parts of the weekend.

The practical takeaway is simple. Today is a use-it day. If you need outdoor time, commutes, errands, or anything easier than what we have had lately, this is the cleaner window. The tradeoff is that it feels cooler than the early-week warmth. Then the atmosphere turns more active again as we move into Friday night and Sunday.

The through-line this morning is that several major stories are leaving the headline phase and entering the proof phase. In the Gulf, the question is whether shipping actually resumes, not whether diplomats sound hopeful. In Washington, the question is whether immigration rhetoric becomes a durable enforcement package. At the Supreme Court, the question is whether a temporary abortion-pill reprieve survives the May 11th deadline. In Columbus, the question is what a 77 percent vote for Issue 5 looks like once implementation begins. And in the Casey Goodson retrial, the question is now entirely in the jury room.

So watch these pressure points today: real vessel traffic through Hormuz, movement on the Senate immigration package, any sign of legal positioning ahead of Monday's mifepristone deadline, the first concrete implementation signals after Issue 5, the pace of jury deliberations in the Meade retrial, whether mortgage pressure eases or worsens after the Freddie Mac uptick, whether AI enthusiasm keeps broadening beyond the usual names, and whether oil's retreat is strong enough to keep markets calm.

That is your Morning Brief for Thursday, May 7th. Have a good morning, use the cooler dry stretch while it is here, and keep an eye on the stories that now need evidence instead of just argument.

item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Tuesday, May 5th, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top national story this morning is that the Strait of Hormuz remains the center of the global risk picture, and the key point is that commerce still has not normalized. Reuters reports that even after the United States said it would begin helping restore freedom of navigation, there were still no signs of a meaningful return in vessel traffic on Monday. MarineTraffic data showed only one tanker, plus a few cargo ships and a cable-laying vessel, moving into the Gulf of Oman. Major commercial operators still do not appear ready to treat the route as safe.

That matters because the continuity in this story is not that Washington has a plan. The continuity is that the market still does not trust the plan yet. Yesterday the question was whether a new American escort effort could restart real shipping. This morning the answer appears to be no, or at least not yet. The industry still lacks clear guidance, insurers and operators are still looking at the Iranian threat, and thousands of seafarers remain stuck in a crisis that has become as much about confidence as about military capacity.

For the U.S. economy, that keeps the inflation risk very much alive. If oil traffic stays constrained, then the pressure runs straight into gasoline prices, freight costs, business margins, inflation expectations, and eventually the mortgage and rate outlook back here at home. So the thing to watch today is not just military rhetoric. It is whether any serious commercial traffic actually resumes. Until that happens, this remains an unresolved economic story, not just a foreign policy story.

The second national story is the next phase of the immigration spending fight. Roll Call reports that two Republican-led Senate committees have now released legislative text for a reconciliation package that would steer about 69.2 billion dollars into Department of Homeland Security enforcement agencies through the rest of President Trump's term. That includes roughly 38.2 billion dollars for ICE and a little more than 26 billion for Customs and Border Protection.

This is the continuity line from the shutdown fight that ended last week. The signed funding bill did not settle the larger enforcement question. It only moved the real fight into a bigger, more ideological package. Now that text is actually on paper, the story is more concrete. This is no longer a vague promise of more enforcement. It is a defined attempt to put a very large amount of money behind detention capacity, personnel, border operations, transport, technology, and related systems.

Politically, this becomes one of the clearest Capitol Hill tests of how aggressively Republicans want to build out the enforcement state while they still have procedural leverage. Practically, it means immigration will stay in the middle of the budget story, not just the campaign story. Watch whether this package gains fast momentum, whether any moderate resistance appears over cost or scope, and whether Democrats decide to attack the proposal mainly on humanitarian grounds, fiscal grounds, or both.

A third national story this morning is the Supreme Court's temporary move on abortion pill access. Reuters reports that Justice Samuel Alito issued an interim order Monday restoring, for now, the federal rule that allows mifepristone to be prescribed through telemedicine and dispensed by mail. That administrative stay runs until May 11 while the justices review emergency requests from the manufacturers after the Fifth Circuit moved to reimpose an in-person requirement.

Why this matters this morning is that the ruling does not resolve the fight, but it does keep the issue fully alive as both a legal and political story. The continuity here is not stability. It is repeated uncertainty. Mail access is back for the moment, but everyone involved now knows another turn is coming quickly. That gives abortion politics a fresh deadline and gives the Court a new test in a case that reaches far beyond one drug. It is about telemedicine, federal regulatory authority, and whether a single state challenge can narrow access nationwide.

So over the next several days, watch the date. May 11 is the current hinge point. If the Court extends the stay, the immediate political temperature may cool a bit. If it does not, this becomes a much sharper national flashpoint almost instantly.

Here in Columbus and Central Ohio, the biggest local story is straightforward. It is election day, and Columbus voters are deciding Issue 5, the charter amendment that would create an alternative crisis response team for non-violent emergencies. Reporting from WOSU through the Ohio Newsroom says the proposal would send teams made up of clinicians, social workers, and EMTs instead of police or firefighters on certain calls, with supporters framing it as a calmer and more specialized response for behavioral-health and similar crises.

The continuity here matters because this story has moved from concept to decision. Yesterday it was still a campaign issue. Today it becomes a turnout issue and, by tonight, a mandate question. If it passes, supporters say the city would get an alternative crisis division running by 2028 with round-the-clock service expected by 2030. That means voters are not just weighing whether the idea sounds good. They are deciding whether Columbus should lock this direction into its charter and force the city to build toward it over the next several years.

The local political read is that Issue 5 has had broader institutional support than many public-safety changes usually get. But today still answers the question that matters most: whether voters want this written into the city's structure, not merely piloted at the mayor's discretion. So watch turnout, vote margin, and whether a yes vote looks like consensus or just narrow approval.

Two other Columbus public-safety stories stay active in the background this morning. The Casey Goodson retrial remains one of the city's most consequential ongoing court cases, and the North Linden police shooting continues to feed accountability arguments around parole supervision and local safety policy. In the Linden case, WOSU reports that police identified the man killed by officers as Chantez Loury and said he had been on supervised parole after an August 2025 prison release. Police leadership sharply criticized the state's corrections system for allegedly losing track of him.

There was not a major overnight turn in either of those stories before this briefing, but both remain important because each could still shape public debate this week. The Goodson retrial is still testing whether jurors accept the prosecution's picture of an unjustified shooting or the defense claim of self-defense. The Linden case remains both a criminal investigation and a political argument about supervision, violent repeat offenders, and police response. In other words, Columbus is voting on one public-safety model while still arguing through two others at the same time.

On home lending and mortgage rates, the headline number from Freddie Mac is still 6.30 percent for the average 30-year fixed mortgage as of April 30, up slightly from 6.23 percent the prior week. Freddie Mac said purchase applications were running more than 20 percent above a year ago, which tells you buyers are still showing up even in a strained affordability environment. But the daily direction is less comfortable. Mortgage News Daily's rate index, updated for May 4, put the top-tier 30-year fixed at 6.56 percent.

That combination is important. The weekly average still says the market is holding roughly steady in the low sixes. The daily market says the latest oil and bond shock is already making borrowing more expensive again. So the continuity here is that housing is surviving, not recovering cleanly. Buyers are still in the market because inventory is better and rates are lower than last year's worst moments, but any renewed jump in yields can still shut the window quickly.

If you are watching this as a homeowner, buyer, or seller, the practical takeaway is simple. The housing market is still extremely sensitive to global risk. A conflict story half a world away is now one of the things shaping whether a borrower in Central Ohio gets a workable monthly payment. Watch Treasury yields, oil, and the next weekly mortgage data because this is exactly the kind of environment where a decent spring market can turn choppy fast.

In AI and technology, the clearest story this morning is not a flashy consumer product launch. It is distribution and enterprise control. A new AWS and OpenAI expansion announced today says the latest OpenAI models, Codex, and managed agents are all coming to Amazon Bedrock in limited preview. That means the AI race keeps moving toward a cloud-platform model where the winning question is less about who had the most viral demo and more about who can make frontier AI usable inside the systems large organizations already trust.

That fits the continuity we have been tracking. The center of gravity in AI is moving toward infrastructure, procurement, governance, and deployment. When OpenAI models and agent tooling become more available inside the AWS environment, it lowers friction for companies that want advanced AI without reorganizing their stack around a single vendor relationship. For investors and business leaders, that is the real signal. Enterprise AI is becoming more portable, more cloud-native, and more operationally embedded.

So the thing to watch now is whether rivals answer with deeper integrations of their own, and whether customers respond more to raw model quality or to the convenience of using advanced models inside the platforms where their data, security controls, and software teams already live.

That brings us to the markets snapshot. Monday was a risk-off day. The Associated Press says the S and P 500 fell 29.37 points to 7,200.75, the Dow dropped 557.37 points to 48,941.90, the Nasdaq slipped 46.64 points to 25,067.80, and the Russell 2000 fell to 2,796.00. The move was tied directly to renewed Middle East escalation and the resulting jump in oil.

The Tuesday morning read is a little calmer, but not exactly calm. Reuters reports that U.S. stock index futures were higher early this morning as oil ticked lower, suggesting investors are trying to recover some confidence after Monday's selloff. That is the key phrase: trying. Markets are being pulled in two directions at once. On one side, strong earnings and AI optimism. On the other side, an oil shock that can reprice inflation and interest-rate expectations very quickly.

So watch whether the market treats Monday as a one-day geopolitical scare or the beginning of a more durable risk repricing. If oil keeps easing and no new major Gulf escalation hits the tape, stocks may stabilize. If shipping remains frozen or attacks widen, bonds, rates, and equities could all move sharply again.

For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service says today should be warm, with a high near 73, but the day gets less stable as it goes on. There is a chance of showers and thunderstorms this morning, then showers become more likely with a possible thunderstorm after about 5 p.m. Tonight stays unsettled, and Wednesday looks cooler with more shower chances before a drier stretch later in the week.

The practical takeaway is easy. If you want the better part of the day, use the middle of it. This is not a washout start to finish, but it is a day with an evening expiration date, and the more unsettled pattern lingers into tomorrow.

The through-line this morning is that several stories have moved past the first headline and into the test phase. In the Gulf, the test is whether commerce actually restarts. In Washington, the test is whether enforcement funding moves from rhetoric into a 69 billion dollar governing project. At the Supreme Court, the test is whether a temporary abortion-pill reprieve becomes something more durable after May 11. In Columbus, the test is literal because voters are deciding whether a different emergency-response model should become part of the city's charter.

So watch these pressure points today: whether commercial ships begin moving in real numbers through Hormuz, whether Senate Republicans quickly advance their immigration package, whether the abortion-pill case hardens into a new legal deadline fight, whether Issue 5 wins decisively or narrowly, whether mortgage markets absorb the oil shock or pass more pain through to borrowers, and whether stocks treat Monday's selloff as a pause or a warning.

That is your Morning Brief for Tuesday, May 5th. Have a good morning, vote if you have not voted yet, use the dry window before evening storms, and keep an eye on the stories that are shifting from argument into measurable consequence.
